levels.title: Literature in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what literature is and trace its path from spoken myths to the modern novel.

levels.title: Myth, Legend, Fable and Folk Tale
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a myth from a legend, a fable (like Aesop's) and a folk tale.

levels.title: Gilgamesh, the Oldest Epic
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the Epic of Gilgamesh and explain its king's failed search for a way to escape death.

levels.title: A Flood Story on a Clay Tablet
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the flood story in Gilgamesh was recognized in 1872 and how it parallels the flood in Genesis.

levels.title: How the World Began
levels.objective: After this level you can compare three common shapes of creation story: order out of chaos, the cosmic egg and the earth diver.

levels.title: Homer: Poems Made to Be Sung
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how oral poets composed epics like Homer's from stock phrases and repeated scenes.

levels.title: Ovid's Metamorphoses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Ovid's poem of transformations became the myth book later writers borrowed from.

levels.title: Hou Yi, Chang'e and the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the Chinese myth of the archer who shot down nine suns and the woman who flew to the Moon.

levels.title: Amaterasu and Japan's Kojiki
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the story of the sun goddess who hid in a cave, from Japan's oldest surviving book.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The First Great Stories
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what myths are and how the oldest stories were composed, written down and passed on.

levels.title: Odin, Thor and Loki
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the main Norse gods and the two Eddas from Iceland that preserved their stories.

levels.title: Ragnarök, the Twilight of the Gods
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the Norse story of the end of the world and its rebirth.

levels.title: The Icelandic Sagas
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the sagas of Icelanders are and why their plain, realistic prose stands out in medieval writing.

levels.title: The Mahabharata
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Mahabharata's war between two sets of cousins and the Bhagavad Gita spoken on its battlefield.

levels.title: The Ramayana
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the Ramayana of Rama, Sita and Hanuman and explain how it spread across South and Southeast Asia.

levels.title: Sundiata, the Epic of Mali
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the epic of Mali's founder and explain how griots have kept it alive by performance.

levels.title: Anansi and the Tricksters
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a trickster is, from Anansi the spider to Coyote and Br'er Rabbit.

levels.title: The Popol Vuh
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the K'iche' Maya story in which the gods try mud and wood before making people from maize.

levels.title: Why Myths Rhyme
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the main theories for why myths from distant places share patterns: shared roots, contact and shared human minds.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Myths Around the World
levels.objective: After this level you can compare myths and epics from Scandinavia, India, Africa and the Americas and spot the patterns they share.

levels.title: The Shape of a Plot
levels.objective: After this level you can identify exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in a story.

levels.title: Conflict Drives the Story
levels.objective: After this level you can name the main kinds of conflict and spot which one drives a story.

levels.title: Round and Flat Characters
levels.objective: After this level you can tell round characters from flat ones and trace a character arc.

levels.title: Who Is Telling the Story?
levels.objective: After this level you can identify first person, third person limited and omniscient narration and what each lets a reader know.

levels.title: Can You Trust the Narrator?
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the clues that a narrator is unreliable.

levels.title: Theme: What a Story Means
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a story's subject from its theme and state a theme in one sentence.

levels.title: Symbols and Motifs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how an object can stand for an idea and how a repeated motif builds meaning.

levels.title: The Hero's Journey
levels.objective: After this level you can trace the stages of Joseph Campbell's hero's journey through a familiar story.

levels.title: Genre: Knowing What to Expect
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a genre sets up promises that readers expect a story to keep or cleverly break.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Stories Work
levels.objective: After this level you can take any story apart into its plot, conflict, characters, narrator and theme.

levels.title: What Makes a Poem a Poem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how line breaks, compression and sound set poetry apart from prose.

levels.title: Rhythm and Meter
levels.objective: After this level you can hear stressed and unstressed syllables and recognize iambic pentameter.

levels.title: Rhyme, Alliteration and Sound
levels.objective: After this level you can identify rhyme, slant rhyme, alliteration and assonance and how each ties words together.

levels.title: Metaphor, Simile and Imagery
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a metaphor from a simile and explain how an image makes a reader feel an idea.

levels.title: The Sonnet
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a sonnet's 14 lines are built in its Italian and English forms and where its turn comes.

levels.title: Haiku
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a haiku captures a single moment, using Basho's poem of the old pond and the frog.

levels.title: Free Verse
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how free verse builds rhythm without regular meter or rhyme.

levels.title: The Epic's Toolkit
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the conventions of epic poetry: calling on the Muse, starting in the middle and the long epic simile.

levels.title: Aristotle's Rules of Tragedy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Aristotle's ideas of the tragic hero's error, the reversal, the recognition and catharsis.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Poetry and Drama Work
levels.objective: After this level you can read a short poem or scene for its meter, sound, imagery and dramatic shape.

levels.title: Antigone: Law Against Conscience
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Sophocles' Antigone, a clash between a ruler's law and a sister's duty to the dead, is still staged.

levels.title: Li Bai, Du Fu and Tang Poetry
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Tang dynasty is called the golden age of Chinese poetry.

levels.title: Journey to the West
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Monkey King's pilgrimage to India became one of China's best-loved novels.

levels.title: The Tale of Genji
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji is often called the world's first novel.

levels.title: The Thousand and One Nights
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Scheherazade tells her stories and how a frame story holds many tales together.

levels.title: The Shahnameh
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Ferdowsi's Book of Kings is credited with keeping the Persian language alive.

levels.title: Beowulf
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Beowulf, which survives in a single manuscript, matters as the great epic of Old English.

levels.title: Dante's Divine Comedy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Dante wrote his journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise in Italian rather than Latin.

levels.title: The Canterbury Tales
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Chaucer's pilgrims telling stories in English made a landmark of English literature.

levels.title: Milestone: Stories That Last
levels.objective: After this level you can connect myths, storytelling craft and the old classics to explain why some stories survive for centuries.

levels.title: Shakespeare's Globe
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare wrote plays that could hold a whole crowd, from standing groundlings to nobles.

levels.title: Hamlet and the Soliloquy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the soliloquy lets an audience hear a character think, using Hamlet.

levels.title: Romeo and Juliet's Borrowed Plot
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare borrowed his plots and what he added to them, using Romeo and Juliet.

levels.title: Disguises and Weddings: Comedies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare's comedies run on disguise and mistaken identity and end in marriage.

levels.title: Words Shakespeare Gave Us
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why so many everyday words and phrases are first recorded in Shakespeare, and what "first recorded" means.

levels.title: Don Quixote
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Cervantes' tale of a man who reads too many knightly romances is called the first modern novel.

levels.title: Why the Novel Took Off
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the novel boomed in 18th-century Britain, from Robinson Crusoe onward.

levels.title: Gulliver and the Art of Satire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why satire uses exaggeration to criticize, using Gulliver's Travels.

levels.title: Jane Austen
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Austen's irony and her way of slipping into a character's thoughts still feel fresh.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Shakespeare and the Novel
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare's plays and the first novels changed what stories could do.

levels.title: The Romantic Poets
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Wordsworth and Coleridge made nature, feeling and everyday speech the stuff of poetry.

levels.title: The Gothic Novel
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Gothic toolkit of old castles, buried secrets and dread, from Walpole to Dracula.

levels.title: Frankenstein, the Modern Prometheus
levels.objective: After this level you can connect Mary Shelley's Frankenstein to the Prometheus myth and to the birth of science fiction.

levels.title: Dickens and the Serial Novel
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how publishing in monthly parts shaped Dickens's cliffhangers, huge casts and fight against poverty.

levels.title: The Brontë Sisters
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Charlotte and Emily Brontë brought passionate inner voices to the novel, and why they first published as men.

levels.title: Realism: Life as It Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how realist novelists like Flaubert and George Eliot made ordinary lives the subject of serious art.

levels.title: Tolstoy's Big Canvas
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how War and Peace and Anna Karenina weave private lives into the history around them.

levels.title: Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Crime and Punishment turns a murder into a psychological drama of guilt and conscience.

levels.title: Ibsen, Chekhov and the Modern Stage
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Ibsen and Chekhov brought ordinary homes and unresolved endings to the stage.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Nineteenth Century
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the Romantics, the Gothic and the great realists into one century's story of the novel and the stage.

levels.title: Poe and the Short Story
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Poe's idea that a short story should build toward a single effect.

levels.title: The Scarlet Letter
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Hawthorne used a symbol to judge the Puritan past.

levels.title: Moby-Dick
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Melville turned a whaling voyage into an epic of obsession.

levels.title: Douglass's Narrative
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Frederick Douglass's 1845 Narrative made reading and writing the road to freedom.

levels.title: Whitman's Leaves of Grass
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Whitman's long free-verse lines tried to hold all of America.

levels.title: Emily Dickinson
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Dickinson packed large ideas into short poems with slant rhyme and dashes.

levels.title: Huckleberry Finn
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Twain's novel told in a boy's own voice changed American writing and still sparks debate.

levels.title: The Harlem Renaissance
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston brought Black speech and music into American literature.

levels.title: Toni Morrison's Beloved
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Morrison's Beloved turns the history of slavery into a story about memory.

levels.title: Checkpoint: American Voices
levels.objective: After this level you can connect American writers from Poe to Morrison into one story of a national literature finding its own voices.

levels.title: Modernism: Make It New
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why writers after World War I broke with traditional plots and forms.

levels.title: Poems from the Trenches
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh how war poets like Wilfred Owen answered the old idea that dying for your country is sweet.

levels.title: The Waste Land
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how T. S. Eliot built a poem from fragments and borrowed voices, and why readers found it hard.

levels.title: Stream of Consciousness
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Joyce and Woolf put a character's flowing thoughts on the page.

levels.title: Kafka's Metamorphosis
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh two readings of Kafka's story of a man who wakes up as an insect.

levels.title: Gatsby and the Lost Generation
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh what The Great Gatsby says about the American Dream.

levels.title: Tagore and Gitanjali
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rabindranath Tagore's songs became the first Nobel-winning work by a writer from outside Europe.

levels.title: Things Fall Apart
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Chinua Achebe wrote back against colonial stories about Africa.

levels.title: Magical Realism
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how magical realism treats the impossible as ordinary, from Gabriel García Márquez's Macondo onward.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Modern and Global
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh what modern writers around the world changed about how stories are told, and why.

levels.title: Fairy Tales Written Down
levels.objective: After this level you can compare versions of a fairy tale by Perrault, the Grimms and Andersen and explain why they differ.

levels.title: Alice and Books for Children
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Lewis Carroll's Alice broke with children's books that preached.

levels.title: The Detective Story
levels.objective: After this level you can use the fair-play rules of detective fiction, from Poe's Dupin to Sherlock Holmes, to spot a planted clue.

levels.title: Science Fiction's Big What If
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Jules Verne and H. G. Wells turned scientific what-ifs into fiction.

levels.title: Dystopias
levels.objective: After this level you can compare how Brave New World and Nineteen Eighty-Four imagine a society controlled by pleasure or by fear.

levels.title: Fantasy and Its Old Myths
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how Tolkien built Middle-earth from Norse myth and Beowulf.

levels.title: Reading in Translation
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh how two translations of the same passage can give a reader different pictures.

levels.title: Myths About Literature
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk common myths, like Frankenstein being the monster's name or someone else writing Shakespeare's plays.

levels.title: Why a Classic Matters
levels.objective: After this level you can use the whole tree to place a classic you pick up in its tradition and explain why it matters.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Literature
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Literature Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
